claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling elicits context-dependent transcription switches that determine normal development and oncogenesis.
source: Wnt/β-catenin signaling elicits context-dependent transcription switches that determine normal development and oncogenesis.
evidence: This is a general statement about Wnt signaling function supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Wnt/β-catenin signaling is mediated by the Wnt enhanceosome, a multiprotein complex binding to the Pygo chromatin reader and acting through TCF/LEF-responsive enhancers.
source: These are mediated by the Wnt enhanceosome, a multiprotein complex binding to the Pygo chromatin reader and acting through TCF/LEF-responsive enhancers.
evidence: This statement describes the mechanism of Wnt signaling based on the authors' previous work and current findings.

claim: Pygo renders the Wnt enhanceosome complex Wnt-responsive by capturing β-catenin via the Legless/BCL9 adaptor.
source: Pygo renders this complex Wnt-responsive, by capturing β-catenin via the Legless/BCL9 adaptor.
evidence: This is a mechanistic claim supported by the authors' experimental findings and previous literature.

claim: The C-terminus downstream of the adaptor elements in Legless/BCL9 is crucial for Wnt responses.
source: We used CRISPR/Cas9 genome engineering of Drosophila legless (lgs) and human BCL9 and B9L to show that the C-terminus downstream of their adaptor elements is crucial for Wnt responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by CRISPR/Cas9 experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: BCL9 and B9L are constitutive components of the Wnt enhanceosome.
source: BioID proximity labeling revealed that BCL9 and B9L, like PYGO2, are constitutive components of the Wnt enhanceosome.
evidence: This claim is supported by BioID proximity labeling experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Wnt-dependent docking of β-catenin to the enhanceosome causes a rearrangement that apposes the BCL9/B9L C-terminus to TCF.
source: Wnt-dependent docking of β-catenin to the enhanceosome apparently causes a rearrangement that apposes the BCL9/B9L C-terminus to TCF.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from BioID data showing Wnt-dependent proximity changes.

claim: The BCL9/B9L C-terminus binds to the Groucho/TLE co-repressor.
source: This C-terminus binds to the Groucho/TLE co-repressor, and also to the Chip/LDB1-SSDP enhanceosome core complex via an evolutionary conserved element.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation and BioID experiments in the manuscript.

claim: The BCL9/B9L C-terminus binds to the Chip/LDB1-SSDP enhanceosome core complex via an evolutionary conserved element.
source: This C-terminus binds to the Groucho/TLE co-repressor, and also to the Chip/LDB1-SSDP enhanceosome core complex via an evolutionary conserved element.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR binding assays and co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: There is a link between BCL9/B9L, PYGO2 and nuclear co-receptor complexes.
source: An unexpected link between BCL9/B9L, PYGO2 and nuclear co-receptor complexes suggests that these β-catenin co-factors may coordinate Wnt and nuclear hormone responses.
evidence: This claim is based on BioID mass spectrometry data identifying nuclear co-receptor components.

claim: The Wnt/β-catenin signaling cascade is an ancient cell communication pathway that operates context-dependent transcriptional switches to control animal development and tissue homeostasis.
source: The Wnt/β-catenin signaling cascade is an ancient cell communication pathway that operates context-dependent transcriptional switches to control animal development and tissue homeostasis (Cadigan and Nusse, 1997).
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field supported by citation.

claim: Deregulation of the Wnt pathway in adult tissues can lead to many different cancers, most notably colorectal cancer.
source: Deregulation of the pathway in adult tissues can lead to many different cancers, most notably colorectal cancer (Clevers and Nusse, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Wnt-induced transcription is mediated by T cell factors (TCF1/3/4, LEF1) bound to Wnt-responsive enhancers.
source: Wnt-induced transcription is mediated by T cell factors (TCF1/3/4, LEF1) bound to Wnt-responsive enhancers, but their activity depends on the co-activator β-catenin (Armadillo in Drosophila), which is rapidly degraded in unstimulated cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Wnt signaling mechanism.

claim: TCF activity depends on the co-activator β-catenin (Armadillo in Drosophila), which is rapidly degraded in unstimulated cells.
source: Wnt-induced transcription is mediated by T cell factors (TCF1/3/4, LEF1) bound to Wnt-responsive enhancers, but their activity depends on the co-activator β-catenin (Armadillo in Drosophila), which is rapidly degraded in unstimulated cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about β-catenin regulation.

claim: Absence of β-catenin defines the OFF state of Wnt-responsive enhancers, which are silenced by Groucho/TLE co-repressors bound to TCF via their Q domain.
source: Absence of β-catenin thus defines the OFF state of these enhancers, which are silenced by Groucho/TLE co-repressors bound to TCF via their Q domain.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The Q domain of Groucho/TLE tetramerizes to promote transcriptional repression.
source: This domain tetramerizes to promote transcriptional repression (Chodaparambil et al., 2014), which leads to chromatin compaction (Sekiya and Zaret, 2007) apparently assisted by the interaction between Groucho/TLE and histone deacetylases (HDACs) (Jennings et al., 2008; Turki-Judeh and Courey, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Groucho/TLE-mediated transcriptional repression leads to chromatin compaction.
source: This domain tetramerizes to promote transcriptional repression (Chodaparambil et al., 2014), which leads to chromatin compaction (Sekiya and Zaret, 2007) apparently assisted by the interaction between Groucho/TLE and histone deacetylases (HDACs) (Jennings et al., 2008; Turki-Judeh and Courey, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Chromatin compaction by Groucho/TLE is assisted by the interaction between Groucho/TLE and histone deacetylases (HDACs).
source: This domain tetramerizes to promote transcriptional repression (Chodaparambil et al., 2014), which leads to chromatin compaction (Sekiya and Zaret, 2007) apparently assisted by the interaction between Groucho/TLE and histone deacetylases (HDACs) (Jennings et al., 2008; Turki-Judeh and Courey, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Wnt signaling relieves Groucho/TLE-mediated repression by blocking the degradation of β-catenin.
source: Wnt signaling relieves this repression by blocking the degradation of β-catenin, which thus accumulates and binds to TCF, converting the Wnt-responsive enhancers into the ON state.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Wnt signaling mechanism.

claim: β-catenin binds to various transcriptional co-activators via its C-terminus, most notably to the CREB-binding protein (CBP) histone acetyltransferase or its p300 paralog.
source: This involves the binding of β-catenin to various transcriptional co-activators via its C-terminus, most notably to the CREB-binding protein (CBP) histone acetyltransferase or its p300 paralog (Mosimann et al., 2009), resulting in the transcription of the linked Wnt target genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Reversion of Wnt-responsive enhancers to the OFF state involves Groucho/TLE-dependent silencing.
source: Subsequent reversion to the OFF state (for example, by negative feedback from high Wnt signaling levels near Wnt-producing cells, or upon cessation of signaling) involves Groucho/TLE-dependent silencing, but also requires the Osa/ARID1 subunit of the BAF (also known as SWI/SNF) chromatin remodeling complex (Collins and Treisman, 2000) which binds to β-catenin through its BRG/BRM subunit (Barker et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Reversion of Wnt-responsive enhancers to the OFF state requires the Osa/ARID1 subunit of the BAF chromatin remodeling complex.
source: Subsequent reversion to the OFF state (for example, by negative feedback from high Wnt signaling levels near Wnt-producing cells, or upon cessation of signaling) involves Groucho/TLE-dependent silencing, but also requires the Osa/ARID1 subunit of the BAF (also known as SWI/SNF) chromatin remodeling complex (Collins and Treisman, 2000) which binds to β-catenin through its BRG/BRM subunit (Barker et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The BAF complex binds to β-catenin through its BRG/BRM subunit.
source: Subsequent reversion to the OFF state (for example, by negative feedback from high Wnt signaling levels near Wnt-producing cells, or upon cessation of signaling) involves Groucho/TLE-dependent silencing, but also requires the Osa/ARID1 subunit of the BAF (also known as SWI/SNF) chromatin remodeling complex (Collins and Treisman, 2000) which binds to β-catenin through its BRG/BRM subunit (Barker et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: More than 20% of all cancers exhibit at least one inactivating mutation in one of the BAF complex subunits, most notably in ARID1A.
source: Cancer genome sequencing has uncovered a widespread tumor suppressor role of the BAF complex, which guards against numerous cancers including colorectal cancer, with >20% of all cancers exhibiting at least one inactivating mutation in one of its subunits, most notably in ARID1A (Kadoch and Crabtree, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to cancer genome sequencing studies.

claim: Failure of Wnt-inducible enhancers to respond to negative feedback imposed by the BAF complex strongly predisposes to cancer.
source: Thus, it appears that failure of Wnt-inducible enhancers to respond to negative feedback imposed by the BAF complex strongly predisposes to cancer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the tumor suppressor role of the BAF complex.

claim: β-catenin and TLE bind to TCF simultaneously.
source: How β-catenin overcomes Groucho/TLE-dependent repression remains unclear, especially since β-catenin and TLE bind to TCF simultaneously (Chodaparambil et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous structural studies.

claim: The simplest model envisaging competition between β-catenin and TLE cannot explain the Wnt switch, which implies that co-factors are required.
source: Therefore, the simplest model envisaging competition between β-catenin and TLE cannot explain this switch, which implies that co-factors are required.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the simultaneous binding of β-catenin and TLE to TCF.

claim: Pygo is a chromatin reader binding to histone H3 tail methylated at lysine 4 (H3K4m) via its C-terminal PHD finger.
source: One of these is Pygo, a chromatin reader binding to histone H3 tail methylated at lysine 4 (H3K4m) via its C-terminal PHD finger (Fiedler et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In Drosophila, Pygo's main function appears to be to assist Armadillo in overcoming Groucho-dependent repression.
source: In Drosophila where Pygo was discovered as an essential co-factor for activated Armadillo, its main function appears to be to assist Armadillo in overcoming Groucho-dependent repression (Mieszczanek et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Pygo associates with TCF enhancers via its highly conserved N-terminal NPF motif that binds directly to the ChiLS complex.
source: We recently discovered that Pygo associates with TCF enhancers via its highly conserved N-terminal NPF motif that binds directly to the ChiLS complex, composed of a dimer of Chip/LDB (LIM domain-binding protein) and a tetramer of SSDP (single-stranded DNA-binding protein, also known as SSBP).
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' recent discovery.

claim: The ChiLS complex is composed of a dimer of Chip/LDB and a tetramer of SSDP.
source: We recently discovered that Pygo associates with TCF enhancers via its highly conserved N-terminal NPF motif that binds directly to the ChiLS complex, composed of a dimer of Chip/LDB (LIM domain-binding protein) and a tetramer of SSDP (single-stranded DNA-binding protein, also known as SSBP).
evidence: This is a structural description of the ChiLS complex.

claim: ChiLS binds to other enhancer-bound NPF factors such as Osa/ARID1 and RUNX.
source: Notably, ChiLS also binds to other enhancer-bound NPF factors such as Osa/ARID1 and RUNX, and to the C-terminal WD40 domain of Groucho/TLE, and thus forms the core module of a multiprotein complex termed 'Wnt enhanceosome' (Fiedler et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: ChiLS binds to the C-terminal WD40 domain of Groucho/TLE.
source: Notably, ChiLS also binds to other enhancer-bound NPF factors such as Osa/ARID1 and RUNX, and to the C-terminal WD40 domain of Groucho/TLE, and thus forms the core module of a multiprotein complex termed 'Wnt enhanceosome' (Fiedler et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: ChiLS forms the core module of a multiprotein complex termed 'Wnt enhanceosome'.
source: Notably, ChiLS also binds to other enhancer-bound NPF factors such as Osa/ARID1 and RUNX, and to the C-terminal WD40 domain of Groucho/TLE, and thus forms the core module of a multiprotein complex termed 'Wnt enhanceosome' (Fiedler et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Pygo renders the Wnt enhanceosome complex Wnt-responsive by capturing Armadillo/β-catenin through the Legless adaptor.
source: We proposed that Pygo renders this complex Wnt-responsive by capturing Armadillo/β-catenin through the Legless adaptor (whose orthologs in humans are BCL9 and B9L, also known as BCL9-2) (Kramps et al., 2002; Städeli and Basler, 2005).
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on previous work.

claim: The Wnt enhanceosome keeps TCF target genes repressed prior to Wnt signaling while at the same time priming them for subsequent Wnt induction.
source: The salient feature of our model is that the Wnt enhanceosome keeps TCF target genes repressed prior to Wnt signaling while at the same time priming them for subsequent Wnt induction, and for timely shut-down via negative feedback depending on Osa/ARID1 (Fiedler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on previous work.

claim: Legless and BCL9/B9L bind to Pygo via their conserved N-terminal homology domain 1 (HD1).
source: Legless and BCL9/B9L paralogs (collectively referred to as Legless/BCL9 below) bind to Pygo and Armadillo/β-catenin via their conserved N-terminal homology domains 1 and 2 (HD1, HD2), respectively (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the domain structure of Legless/BCL9, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Legless and BCL9/B9L bind to Armadillo/β-catenin via their conserved homology domain 2 (HD2).
source: Legless and BCL9/B9L paralogs (collectively referred to as Legless/BCL9 below) bind to Pygo and Armadillo/β-catenin via their conserved N-terminal homology domains 1 and 2 (HD1, HD2), respectively (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the domain structure of Legless/BCL9, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Previous evidence suggested that the sole function of Legless during Drosophila development is to link Pygo to Armadillo.
source: Previous evidence suggested that the sole function of Legless during Drosophila development is to link Pygo to Armadillo (Kramps et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim summarizes previous findings from the literature.

claim: C-terminal truncations of BCL9/B9L behave as dominant-negatives regarding Wnt responses in mammalian cell lines.
source: However, C-terminal truncations of BCL9/B9L behave as dominant-negatives regarding Wnt responses in mammalian cell lines (Adachi et al., 2004; de la Roche et al., 2008), which suggested that their C-termini harbor functionally relevant elements.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The lgs7I mutation encodes a Legless truncation with a stop codon downstream of HD2.
source: Indeed, these elements are missing in a Legless truncation encoded by a known lgs mutation (lgs7I), owing to a stop codon downstream of HD2 (Kramps et al., 2002), yet this truncation should be fully competent to link Pygo to Armadillo.
evidence: This is a description of a known mutation from the literature.

claim: The C-termini of Legless/BCL9 exhibit several conserved sequence blocks, in particular HD3.
source: Consistent with the notion of functional elements downstream of HD2, the C-termini of Legless/BCL9 exhibit several conserved sequence blocks, in particular HD3 (Figure 1A) which is found in all orthologs from the most primitive animals to humans.
evidence: This is an observation about sequence conservation illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: HD3 is found in all Legless/BCL9 orthologs from the most primitive animals to humans.
source: Consistent with the notion of functional elements downstream of HD2, the C-termini of Legless/BCL9 exhibit several conserved sequence blocks, in particular HD3 (Figure 1A) which is found in all orthologs from the most primitive animals to humans.
evidence: This is an observation about evolutionary conservation.

claim: No ligand has been identified for HD3 prior to this study.
source: No ligand has been identified for HD3, nor for the C-terminus of Legless/BCL9.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to the current study.

claim: The lgs2-8 truncation allele causes pupal lethality if combined with a strong lgs allele (lgs20F).
source: Notably, the lgs2-8 truncation allele causes pupal lethality if combined with a strong lgs allele (lgs20F; Kramps et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a genetic observation from experiments in Drosophila.

claim: Homozygous lgs2-8 animals show severely delayed development.
source: Furthermore, homozygous lgs2-8 animals (derived from homozygous mothers) show severely delayed development, and most die in their pupal cases, with <25% of them hatching as flies (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a phenotypic observation shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Most homozygous lgs2-8 animals die in their pupal cases, with less than 25% hatching as flies.
source: Furthermore, homozygous lgs2-8 animals (derived from homozygous mothers) show severely delayed development, and most die in their pupal cases, with <25% of them hatching as flies (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A high fraction of lgs2-8 escaper flies exhibit patterning defects indicative of attenuated Wingless signaling.
source: A high fraction of these escapers exhibit patterning defects indicative of attenuated signaling by Wingless (Wg, Drosophila Wnt), as previously observed in flies bearing weak alleles of lgs, pygo, and dTCF (Brunner et al., 1997; Kramps et al., 2002; Thompson et al., 2002)—namely proximal leg duplications and dorso-ventral polarity leg defects (in ~1/2 mutant flies) as well as loss of sternites in the ventral abdomen (in ~1/6 mutant flies; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a phenotypic observation shown in Figure 1D and compared to previous literature.

claim: Approximately half of lgs2-8 mutant flies exhibit proximal leg duplications and dorso-ventral polarity leg defects.
source: A high fraction of these escapers exhibit patterning defects indicative of attenuated signaling by Wingless (Wg, Drosophila Wnt), as previously observed in flies bearing weak alleles of lgs, pygo, and dTCF (Brunner et al., 1997; Kramps et al., 2002; Thompson et al., 2002)—namely proximal leg duplications and dorso-ventral polarity leg defects (in ~1/2 mutant flies) as well as loss of sternites in the ventral abdomen (in ~1/6 mutant flies; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative phenotypic observation shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Approximately one-sixth of lgs2-8 mutant flies exhibit loss of sternites in the ventral abdomen.
source: A high fraction of these escapers exhibit patterning defects indicative of attenuated signaling by Wingless (Wg, Drosophila Wnt), as previously observed in flies bearing weak alleles of lgs, pygo, and dTCF (Brunner et al., 1997; Kramps et al., 2002; Thompson et al., 2002)—namely proximal leg duplications and dorso-ventral polarity leg defects (in ~1/2 mutant flies) as well as loss of sternites in the ventral abdomen (in ~1/6 mutant flies; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a quantitative phenotypic observation shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The sequences downstream of HD2 in Legless are essential for Drosophila development.
source: Thus, the sequences downstream of HD2 are essential for Drosophila development, and appear to participate in Wg signaling responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the phenotypic analysis of lgs2-8 mutants.

claim: The sequences downstream of HD2 in Legless appear to participate in Wg signaling responses.
source: Thus, the sequences downstream of HD2 are essential for Drosophila development, and appear to participate in Wg signaling responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the phenotypic analysis showing Wg-like defects.

claim: More than one-third of leg discs from lgs2-8 homozygotes show derepression of dpp.lacZ in the ventral compartment.
source: Immunofluorescence revealed a striking derepression of dpp.lacZ in the ventral compartment of >1/3 of the leg discs from lgs2-8 homozygotes (28/78 discs) (Figure 2A,B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that the function of the mutant Legless in transducing the Wg signal is severely compromised in these discs.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The function of the mutant Legless in transducing the Wg signal is severely compromised in lgs2-8 leg discs.
source: Immunofluorescence revealed a striking derepression of dpp.lacZ in the ventral compartment of >1/3 of the leg discs from lgs2-8 homozygotes (28/78 discs) (Figure 2A,B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that the function of the mutant Legless in transducing the Wg signal is severely compromised in these discs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the derepression of dpp.lacZ.

claim: Wing discs from lgs2-8 homozygotes exhibit much reduced expression of Senseless.
source: This was also true for wing discs (dissected from of pupating larvae, to ensure matched developmental timing between mutants and wild-type, wt): these discs exhibit much reduced expression of Senseless (Sens) (n = 50 discs; Figure 2C,D), a Wg target gene that specifies bristles along the wing margin and whose expression is abolished in pygo mutant clones (Parker et al., 2002; Fiedler et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an observation from immunofluorescence experiments shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Senseless is a Wg target gene that specifies bristles along the wing margin.
source: This was also true for wing discs (dissected from of pupating larvae, to ensure matched developmental timing between mutants and wild-type, wt): these discs exhibit much reduced expression of Senseless (Sens) (n = 50 discs; Figure 2C,D), a Wg target gene that specifies bristles along the wing margin and whose expression is abolished in pygo mutant clones (Parker et al., 2002; Fiedler et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Senseless expression is abolished in pygo mutant clones.
source: This was also true for wing discs (dissected from of pupating larvae, to ensure matched developmental timing between mutants and wild-type, wt): these discs exhibit much reduced expression of Senseless (Sens) (n = 50 discs; Figure 2C,D), a Wg target gene that specifies bristles along the wing margin and whose expression is abolished in pygo mutant clones (Parker et al., 2002; Fiedler et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a fact from previous literature supported by citations.

claim: Attenuation of Senseless results in fewer margin bristles in homozygous lgs2-8 escaper flies.
source: As expected, this attenuation of Sens results in fewer margin bristles in the homozygous mutant escaper flies (61 versus 80 stout margin bristles, and 15.6 versus 18.8 chemosensory bristles, per wt versus mutant wing, respectively), and larger gaps between individual stout bristles (22.7 versus 17.3 μm, per mutant versus wt wing, respectively) (Figure 2E,F; mean values from 10 wings dissected from different homozygous lgs2-8 females; the sizes of wt and mutant wings were the same).

source: As expected, this attenuation of Sens results in fewer margin bristles in the homozygous mutant escaper flies (61 versus 80 stout margin bristles, and 15.6 versus 18.8 chemosensory bristles, per wt versus mutant wing, respectively), and larger gaps between individual stout bristles (22.7 versus 17.3 μm, per mutant versus wt wing, respectively) (Figure 2E,F; mean values from 10 wings dissected from different homozygous lgs2-8 females; the sizes of wt and mutant wings were the same).
