claim: RT-qPCR assays show significant reductions in the expression levels of engrailed, Distalless and H15 in lgs2-8 wing discs compared to controls.
source: We also used RT-qPCR to examine RNA expression levels of the endogenous Wg target genes engrailed, Distalless and H15 (Cadigan and Nusse, 1997; Estella et al., 2008; Wilder and Perrimon, 1995) in lysates from wing discs dissected from climbing (that is, fully grown) homozygous lgs2-8 larvae. We found significant reductions in the expression levels of all three target genes compared to controls (Figure 2G; note that neither dpp nor dpp.lacZ expression is controlled by Wg in wings discs; see Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from RT-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Neither dpp nor dpp.lacZ expression is controlled by Wg in wing discs.
source: We also used RT-qPCR to examine RNA expression levels of the endogenous Wg target genes engrailed, Distalless and H15 (Cadigan and Nusse, 1997; Estella et al., 2008; Wilder and Perrimon, 1995) in lysates from wing discs dissected from climbing (that is, fully grown) homozygous lgs2-8 larvae. We found significant reductions in the expression levels of all three target genes compared to controls (Figure 2G; note that neither dpp nor dpp.lacZ expression is controlled by Wg in wings discs; see Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is an observation about gene regulation in wing discs.

claim: Heterozygosity of lgs2-8 suppresses the rough eye phenotype caused by activated Armadillo.
source: Finally, we also found that heterozygosity of lgs2-8 suppresses the rough eye phenotype caused by activated Armadillo (Freeman and Bienz, 2001), indistinguishably from heterozygosity of pygoS123 or lgs20F (Thompson et al., 2002; Kramps et al., 2002) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a genetic observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The C-terminal Legless truncation encoded by lgs2-8 is severely compromised in its ability to transduce the Wg signal in multiple developmental contexts.
source: These results demonstrate that the C-terminal Legless truncation encoded by our lgs2-8 allele is severely compromised in its ability to transduce the Wg signal in multiple developmental contexts, despite retaining normal adaptor function in linking Pygo and Armadillo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of experimental evidence.

claim: The lgs2-8 truncation retains normal adaptor function in linking Pygo and Armadillo.
source: These results demonstrate that the C-terminal Legless truncation encoded by our lgs2-8 allele is severely compromised in its ability to transduce the Wg signal in multiple developmental contexts, despite retaining normal adaptor function in linking Pygo and Armadillo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the domain structure of the lgs2-8 truncation.

claim: The adaptor function of Legless is not sufficient to sustain normal development if Legless is expressed at endogenous levels.
source: Evidently, this adaptor function is not sufficient to sustain normal development if Legless is expressed at endogenous levels, suggesting that the previously reported rescue activities of equivalent Legless fragments (Kramps et al., 2002) may have stemmed from overexpression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lgs2-8 phenotype and comparison to previous literature.

claim: Approximately 5% of homozygous lgsΔHD3 flies exhibit leg abnormalities similar to those exhibited by lgs2-8.
source: We also examined homozygous lgsΔHD3 animals, which hatched as flies without showing any developmental delay (Figure 1C). However, ~5% of these flies exhibited leg abnormalities, similarly to those exhibited by lgs2-8 (Figure 1D) although the penetrance of this phenotype was much higher in the latter (see above).
evidence: This is a quantitative phenotypic observation shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Leg defects in lgsΔHD3 homozygotes suggest that HD3 contributes to the function of Legless in transducing Wg responses.
source: Nevertheless, these leg defects in the lgsΔHD3 homozygotes suggest that HD3 contributes to the function of Legless in transducing Wg responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the phenotypic analysis of lgsΔHD3 mutants.

claim: The Wnt-induced transcriptional activity of BCL9/B9L double knock-out HEK293T cells is reduced to less than 20% of their parental control cells.
source: Using a TCF-dependent reporter assay (called SuperTOP; Veeman et al., 2003), we found the Wnt-induced transcriptional activity of these DKO cells to be substantially reduced (to <20% of their parental control cells; Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from reporter assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Loss of BCL9 reduces the transcriptional activity nearly as much as loss of both BCL9 and B9L paralogs.
source: Loss of BCL9 reduces the transcriptional activity nearly as much as loss of both paralogs, suggesting that BCL9 may be the physiologically limiting paralog in these cells, at least for transient Wnt responses.
evidence: This is an observation from reporter assays comparing single and double knock-outs.

claim: BCL9 may be the physiologically limiting paralog in HEK293T cells for transient Wnt responses.
source: Loss of BCL9 reduces the transcriptional activity nearly as much as loss of both paralogs, suggesting that BCL9 may be the physiologically limiting paralog in these cells, at least for transient Wnt responses.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the comparison of single and double knock-out phenotypes.

claim: The endogenous Wnt target genes AXIN2 and SP5 are no longer Wnt-inducible in BCL9/B9L double knock-out cells.
source: Likewise, the endogenous Wnt target genes AXIN2 (Lustig et al., 2002) and SP5 (Hoverter et al., 2012; Weidinger et al., 2005) are no longer Wnt-inducible in the DKO cells (Figure 3B), reconfirming the critical role of BCL9/B9L in the Wnt response of these cells.
evidence: This is an observation from RT-qPCR experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Re-expression of FLAG-B9L in BCL9/B9L double knock-out cells restores full Wnt-responsiveness.
source: When we re-expressed FLAG-B9L in the DKO cells, this restored full Wnt-responsiveness (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an observation from rescue experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: C-terminal truncation mutants of B9L (△C, △HD3△C) fail to restore Wnt-responsiveness in BCL9/B9L double knock-out cells.
source: However, the C-terminal truncation mutants of B9L (△C, △HD3△C) failed to do so (despite elevated expression levels in the case of △HD3△C), and the HD3 deletion provided only partial rescue activity, similarly to a deletion mutant lacking the HD1 Pygo-binding element (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an observation from rescue experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The HD3 deletion in B9L provides only partial rescue activity in BCL9/B9L double knock-out cells.
source: However, the C-terminal truncation mutants of B9L (△C, △HD3△C) failed to do so (despite elevated expression levels in the case of △HD3△C), and the HD3 deletion provided only partial rescue activity, similarly to a deletion mutant lacking the HD1 Pygo-binding element (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an observation from rescue experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The B9L C-terminus is crucial for the Wnt response of HEK293T cells.
source: This demonstrates the crucial role of the B9L C-terminus for the Wnt response of these cells, and it indicates a functional contribution of HD3 to this response.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rescue experiments with B9L mutants.

claim: HD3 makes a functional contribution to the Wnt response in HEK293T cells.
source: This demonstrates the crucial role of the B9L C-terminus for the Wnt response of these cells, and it indicates a functional contribution of HD3 to this response.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the partial rescue activity of the HD3 deletion.

claim: Re-expressed GFP-BCL9 restores Wnt-responsiveness in BCL9/B9L double knock-out cells.
source: Restoration of Wnt-responsiveness is also provided by re-expressed BCL9 tagged with green fluorescent protein (GFP-BCL9) albeit not by its C-terminal truncation, but we did not analyze this paralog further since its transcriptional activation potential is not as strong as that of the nuclear B9L (de la Roche et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an observation from rescue experiments.

claim: The C-terminal truncation of GFP-BCL9 does not restore Wnt-responsiveness in BCL9/B9L double knock-out cells.
source: Restoration of Wnt-responsiveness is also provided by re-expressed BCL9 tagged with green fluorescent protein (GFP-BCL9) albeit not by its C-terminal truncation, but we did not analyze this paralog further since its transcriptional activation potential is not as strong as that of the nuclear B9L (de la Roche et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an observation from rescue experiments.

claim: The transcriptional activation potential of BCL9 is not as strong as that of the nuclear B9L.
source: Restoration of Wnt-responsiveness is also provided by re-expressed BCL9 tagged with green fluorescent protein (GFP-BCL9) albeit not by its C-terminal truncation, but we did not analyze this paralog further since its transcriptional activation potential is not as strong as that of the nuclear B9L (de la Roche et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a fact from previous literature supported by citation.

claim: BioID experiments with B9L-BirA* consistently identified ARID1A and ARID1B as the top hits.
source: Strikingly, each experiment identified known components of the Wnt enhanceosome, even in the absence of Wnt stimulation: we consistently found ARID1A and ARID1B as the top hits, followed closely by TLE3, TLE1, TLE4, LDB1 and PYGO2 and, further down the list, TCF factors, β-catenin and SSBP3/4 (initially named SSDP1/2; the peptides obtained do not distinguish between these closely related paralogs) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: BioID experiments with B9L-BirA* identified TLE3, TLE1, TLE4, LDB1 and PYGO2 as hits following closely after ARID1A/B.
source: Strikingly, each experiment identified known components of the Wnt enhanceosome, even in the absence of Wnt stimulation: we consistently found ARID1A and ARID1B as the top hits, followed closely by TLE3, TLE1, TLE4, LDB1 and PYGO2 and, further down the list, TCF factors, β-catenin and SSBP3/4 (initially named SSDP1/2; the peptides obtained do not distinguish between these closely related paralogs) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: BioID experiments with B9L-BirA* identified TCF factors, β-catenin and SSBP3/4 further down the list of hits.
source: Strikingly, each experiment identified known components of the Wnt enhanceosome, even in the absence of Wnt stimulation: we consistently found ARID1A and ARID1B as the top hits, followed closely by TLE3, TLE1, TLE4, LDB1 and PYGO2 and, further down the list, TCF factors, β-catenin and SSBP3/4 (initially named SSDP1/2; the peptides obtained do not distinguish between these closely related paralogs) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: BioID experiments with B9L-BirA* identified nine additional subunits of the BAF complex.
source: We also found nine additional subunits of the BAF complex (Kadoch and Crabtree, 2015) on our list, topped by BRG-1/SMARCA4, with only BAF155/SMARCC1, BAF47/SMARCB1, SS18 and BCL7 missing (the latter three likely for technical reasons; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The fully assembled BAF complex is tethered to the Wnt enhanceosome, presumably through its enhancer-binding Osa/ARID1 subunit which also binds to ChiLS.
source: This indicates that the fully assembled BAF complex is tethered to the Wnt enhanceosome, presumably through its enhancer-binding Osa/ARID1 subunit which also binds to ChiLS (see Introduction).
evidence: This is an inference based on the BioID data and previous knowledge about ARID1 binding to ChiLS.

claim: BioID experiments with B9L-BirA* identified the CBP co-activator and its p300 paralog.
source: Furthermore, we found the CBP co-activator and its p300 paralog, as well as DNA-binding proteins of the LHX and GATA families known to tether ChiLS to DNA (Love et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments.

claim: BioID experiments with B9L-BirA* identified DNA-binding proteins of the LHX and GATA families known to tether ChiLS to DNA.
source: Furthermore, we found the CBP co-activator and its p300 paralog, as well as DNA-binding proteins of the LHX and GATA families known to tether ChiLS to DNA (Love et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments, with the function of LHX and GATA proteins supported by citation.

claim: Essentially the same set of proteins were found with BCL9-BirA* as a bait, albeit with lower efficiency.
source: Essentially the same set of proteins were found with BCL9-BirA* as a bait, albeit with lower efficiency (Figure 4B), possibly because of its largely cytoplasmic localization.
evidence: This is an observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The lower efficiency of BCL9-BirA* in BioID experiments is possibly because of its largely cytoplasmic localization.
source: Essentially the same set of proteins were found with BCL9-BirA* as a bait, albeit with lower efficiency (Figure 4B), possibly because of its largely cytoplasmic localization.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known subcellular distribution of BCL9.

claim: Several cytoplasmic proteins are specifically associated with BCL9 but not B9L, including α-catenin.
source: Indeed, we found several cytoplasmic proteins specifically associated with BCL9 but not B9L, including α-catenin (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: RIME experiments with B9L-BirA* identified only five specific hits: PYGO2, LDB1, TLE3, CBP, and QKI.
source: These RIME experiments identified only five specific hits; these proteins associated with B9L-BirA* (Figure 4C) include PYGO2, its only known direct ligand in the absence of Wnt.
evidence: This is an observation from RIME experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: PYGO2 is the only known direct ligand of B9L in the absence of Wnt.
source: These RIME experiments identified only five specific hits; these proteins associated with B9L-BirA* (Figure 4C) include PYGO2, its only known direct ligand in the absence of Wnt.
evidence: This is established knowledge about B9L interactions.

claim: The RIME hit list for B9L-BirA* contained LDB1, which is identified as a direct B9L ligand.
source: This short list also contained LDB1, which we shall identify below as another direct B9L ligand.
evidence: This is a forward reference to results presented later in the manuscript.

claim: TLE3 topped the RIME hit list for B9L-BirA*, suggesting that TLE3 may be a direct ligand of B9L.
source: It was topped by TLE3, suggesting that TLE3 may also be a direct ligand of B9L.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the RIME results.

claim: The majority of the hits identified by B9L-BirA* or BCL9-BirA* hardly change after Wnt stimulation.
source: Importantly, the majority of the hits identified by B9L-BirA* or BCL9-BirA* hardly change after Wnt stimulation (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is an observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: BCL9/B9L is associated with the Wnt enhanceosome prior to Wnt stimulation and independently of β-catenin.
source: This implies that BCL9/B9L is associated with the Wnt enhanceosome prior to Wnt stimulation and independently of β-catenin.
evidence: This is an inference based on the BioID data showing Wnt-independent association.

claim: The spectral counts of many BioID hits tend to be slightly increased upon Wnt signaling.
source: We note however that the spectral counts of many hits tend to be slightly increased upon Wnt signaling, a trend that is also apparent for TLE1 and TLE3 whose labeling by B9L-BirA* was increased 2-3x upon Wnt stimulation (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is an observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The labeling of TLE1 and TLE3 by B9L-BirA* was increased 2-3x upon Wnt stimulation.
source: We note however that the spectral counts of many hits tend to be slightly increased upon Wnt signaling, a trend that is also apparent for TLE1 and TLE3 whose labeling by B9L-BirA* was increased 2-3x upon Wnt stimulation (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The labeling of GSE1 by B9L-BirA* is increased 3-5x in Wnt-stimulated cells.
source: Similarly, the labeling of GSE1 by B9L-BirA* is increased 3-5x in stimulated cells (Figure 4A): GSE1 is a subunit of the BRAF-HDAC complex (also known as BHC) (Hakimi et al., 2003), which might interact with Groucho/TLE through its HDAC subunit, potentially explaining the Wnt-dependent increase in the labeling of GSE1.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: GSE1 is a subunit of the BRAF-HDAC complex.
source: Similarly, the labeling of GSE1 by B9L-BirA* is increased 3-5x in stimulated cells (Figure 4A): GSE1 is a subunit of the BRAF-HDAC complex (also known as BHC) (Hakimi et al., 2003), which might interact with Groucho/TLE through its HDAC subunit, potentially explaining the Wnt-dependent increase in the labeling of GSE1.
evidence: This is a fact from previous literature supported by citation.

claim: The BRAF-HDAC complex might interact with Groucho/TLE through its HDAC subunit.
source: Similarly, the labeling of GSE1 by B9L-BirA* is increased 3-5x in stimulated cells (Figure 4A): GSE1 is a subunit of the BRAF-HDAC complex (also known as BHC) (Hakimi et al., 2003), which might interact with Groucho/TLE through its HDAC subunit, potentially explaining the Wnt-dependent increase in the labeling of GSE1.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the Wnt-dependent increase in GSE1 labeling.

claim: TLE1/3 remains associated with Wnt-responsive enhancers even when these are active.
source: In any case, TLE1/3 behaves like the LDB1 core component of the Wnt enhanceosome in remaining associated with Wnt-responsive enhancers even when these are active, consistent with recent findings that TLE1 and β-catenin can bind simultaneously to TCF1 (Chodaparambil et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the BioID data and supported by citation to previous structural studies.

claim: TLE1 and β-catenin can bind simultaneously to TCF1.
source: In any case, TLE1/3 behaves like the LDB1 core component of the Wnt enhanceosome in remaining associated with Wnt-responsive enhancers even when these are active, consistent with recent findings that TLE1 and β-catenin can bind simultaneously to TCF1 (Chodaparambil et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a fact from previous literature supported by citation.

claim: Association of β-catenin with BCL9/B9L is undetectable prior to Wnt stimulation.
source: Association of β-catenin with BCL9/B9L is undetectable prior to Wnt stimulation, as expected from its low abundance in the absence of signaling.
evidence: This is an observation from BioID experiments explained by the known regulation of β-catenin.

claim: The labeling of CBP and p300 by B9L-BirA* is stimulated approximately 4-6x upon Wnt stimulation.
source: This may also explain why the labeling of CBP and p300 by B9L-BirA* is stimulated ~4–6x upon Wnt stimulation, given that these histone acetyltransferases are known ligands of β-catenin.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments.

claim: CBP and p300 are known ligands of β-catenin.
source: This may also explain why the labeling of CBP and p300 by B9L-BirA* is stimulated ~4–6x upon Wnt stimulation, given that these histone acetyltransferases are known ligands of β-catenin.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: CBP and p300 exhibit a significant level of labeling by B9L-BirA* even without Wnt signaling.
source: However, both proteins exhibit a significant level of labeling even without Wnt signaling, suggesting a constitutive association with the Wnt enhanceosome, consistent with the identification of CBP by RIME as a putative direct ligand of B9L.
evidence: This is an observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments.

claim: CBP and p300 have a constitutive association with the Wnt enhanceosome.
source: However, both proteins exhibit a significant level of labeling even without Wnt signaling, suggesting a constitutive association with the Wnt enhanceosome, consistent with the identification of CBP by RIME as a putative direct ligand of B9L.
evidence: This is an inference based on the BioID data showing Wnt-independent labeling.

claim: The binding of CBP and p300 to β-catenin upon its docking to the Wnt enhanceosome increases their proximity to the C-terminus of BCL9/B9L.
source: It thus appears that the binding of CBP and p300 to β-catenin upon its docking to the Wnt enhanceosome increases their proximity to the C-terminus of BCL9/B9L, which bears the BirA* tag.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Wnt-inducible increase in CBP/p300 labeling.

claim: The labeling of TCF4 by B9L-BirA* is Wnt-inducible by 13x.
source: TCF4 is the only TCF paralog labeled prior to Wnt signaling, albeit at very low levels (also by the BirA* control), but its labeling by B9L-BirA* or BCL9-BirA* is Wnt-inducible by 13x or 2.5x, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments.

claim: The labeling of TCF4 by BCL9-BirA* is Wnt-inducible by 2.5x.
source: TCF4 is the only TCF paralog labeled prior to Wnt signaling, albeit at very low levels (also by the BirA* control), but its labeling by B9L-BirA* or BCL9-BirA* is Wnt-inducible by 13x or 2.5x, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments.

claim: For TCF1/3 and LEF1, no labeling is detectable in unstimulated cells, whereas each of these factors is labeled efficiently upon Wnt signaling (>19–30x).
source: For TCF1/3 and LEF1, no labeling is detectable in unstimulated cells, whereas each of these factors is labeled efficiently upon Wnt signaling (>19–30x).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments.

claim: APC is a BCL9-specific BioID hit that is recruited to TCF target genes upon Wnt signaling by β-catenin.
source: The same is true for the APC tumor suppressor (>29x), a BCL9-specific hit that is recruited to TCF target genes upon Wnt signaling by β-catenin (Sierra et al., 2006), owing to direct high-affinity binding (Choi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an observation from BioID experiments supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: APC binds directly to β-catenin with high affinity.
source: The same is true for the APC tumor suppressor (>29x), a BCL9-specific hit that is recruited to TCF target genes upon Wnt signaling by β-catenin (Sierra et al., 2006), owing to direct high-affinity binding (Choi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a fact from previous literature supported by citation.

claim: The labeling of SSBP3/4 by B9L-BirA* is moderately increased (>6x) in Wnt-stimulated cells.
source: Finally, the labeling of SSBP3/4 by B9L-BirA* is moderately increased (>6x) in Wnt-stimulated cells; as in the case of CBP/p300, SSBP3/4 is also detectable prior to Wnt signaling, albeit close to background levels.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments.

claim: SSBP3/4 is detectable by B9L-BirA* prior to Wnt signaling, albeit close to background levels.
source: Finally, the labeling of SSBP3/4 by B9L-BirA* is moderately increased (>6x) in Wnt-stimulated cells; as in the case of CBP/p300, SSBP3/4 is also detectable prior to Wnt signaling, albeit close to background levels.
evidence: This is an observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments.

claim: Wnt signaling or β-catenin induces the proximity of APC, SSBP3/4 and TCF factors to the C-terminus of BCL9/B9L.
source: Therefore, a likely explanation for the Wnt-inducible labeling of these factors is that Wnt signaling, or β-catenin, induces their proximity to the C-terminus of BCL9/B9L.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Wnt-inducible labeling patterns in BioID experiments.

claim: TCF factors are bound constitutively to their cognate enhancers.
source: We note that TCF factors are bound constitutively to their cognate enhancers (for example, TCF4 in unstimulated HEK293 cells; Frietze et al., 2012) although, in Drosophila, the association of dTCF with Wg-responsive enhancers appears to be strengthened by Wg signaling (Parker et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a fact from previous literature supported by citation.

claim: In Drosophila, the association of dTCF with Wg-responsive enhancers appears to be strengthened by Wg signaling.
source: We note that TCF factors are bound constitutively to their cognate enhancers (for example, TCF4 in unstimulated HEK293 cells; Frietze et al., 2012) although, in Drosophila, the association of dTCF with Wg-responsive enhancers appears to be strengthened by Wg signaling (Parker et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a fact from previous literature supported by citation.

claim: FLAG-B9L and GFP-TCF4 co-immunoprecipitate with similar efficiency in cells with or without Wnt stimulation.
source: To obtain independent evidence for the constitutive association between BCL9/B9L and TCF, we conducted coIP assays in HEK293T cells co-expressing FLAG-B9L and GFP-TCF4. As expected, the two proteins coIP with similar efficiency in cells with or without Wnt stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: CoIP of GFP-BCL9 with endogenous PYGO2 is Wnt-independent.
source: Likewise, coIP of GFP-BCL9 with endogenous PYGO2 is also Wnt-independent, whereas its coIP with endogenous β-catenin (or activated β-catenin, ABC) is strictly Wnt-inducible, as expected (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: CoIP of GFP-BCL9 with endogenous β-catenin is strictly Wnt-inducible.
source: Likewise, coIP of GFP-BCL9 with endogenous PYGO2 is also Wnt-independent, whereas its coIP with endogenous β-catenin (or activated β-catenin, ABC) is strictly Wnt-inducible, as expected (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The Wnt-inducible labeling of TCF factors by B9L-BirA* and BCL9-BirA* reflects β-catenin-dependent apposition of the C-terminus of BCL9/B9L to TCF, rather than β-catenin-dependent recruitment of Legless/BCL9 to TCF.
source: This underscores our notion that the Wnt-inducible labeling of TCF factors by B9L-BirA* and BCL9-BirA* reflects β-catenin-dependent apposition of the C-terminus of BCL9/B9L to TCF, rather than β-catenin-dependent recruitment of Legless/BCL9 to TCF (as initially envisaged; Kramps et al., 2002; Städeli and Basler, 2005).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the BioID and coIP data, contrasting with previous models.

claim: PYGO2-BirA* identified the same Wnt enhanceosome components as B9L-BirA*, with ARID1A/B topping the list.
source: By and large, PYGO2-BirA* identified the same Wnt enhanceosome components as B9L-BirA*, with ARID1A/B topping the list (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: SSBP3/4 was labeled more efficiently by PYGO2-BirA* than by B9L-BirA*.
source: SSBP3/4 was labeled more efficiently by PYGO2-BirA* than by B9L-BirA*, consistent with our evidence that Pygo binds directly to an interface shared between LDB1 and SSDP (Fiedler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments consistent with previous findings.

claim: Pygo binds directly to an interface shared between LDB1 and SSDP.
source: SSBP3/4 was labeled more efficiently by PYGO2-BirA* than by B9L-BirA*, consistent with our evidence that Pygo binds directly to an interface shared between LDB1 and SSDP (Fiedler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a fact from previous work by the authors supported by citation.

claim: The labeling of p300 and CBP by PYGO2-BirA* was moderately Wnt-inducible (~3x).
source: Importantly, except for p300 and CBP whose labeling by PYGO2-BirA* was moderately Wnt-inducible (~3x), all other components of the Wnt enhanceosome and BAF complex were labeled with similar efficiency regardless of Wnt signaling, including TCF1/3/4 and LEF1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: All components of the Wnt enhanceosome and BAF complex except p300 and CBP were labeled by PYGO2-BirA* with similar efficiency regardless of Wnt signaling.
source: Importantly, except for p300 and CBP whose labeling by PYGO2-BirA* was moderately Wnt-inducible (~3x), all other components of the Wnt enhanceosome and BAF complex were labeled with similar efficiency regardless of Wnt signaling, including TCF1/3/4 and LEF1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The proximity of PYGO2 to TCF factors does not change as a result of β-catenin docking the Wnt enhanceosome.
source: Thus, the proximity of PYGO2 to TCF factors does not change as a result of β-catenin docking the Wnt enhanceosome.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the BioID data showing Wnt-independent labeling of TCF factors by PYGO2-BirA*.

claim: BCL9ΔC barely associates with TLE1 or TLE3.
source: The lists of proteins associated with △C baits are similar to those found with the wt, but a few of them show reduced spectral counts, most notably in the case of BCL9ΔC which barely associates with TLE1 nor TLE3 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The C-terminal WD40 domain of TLE3 is both necessary and sufficient for co-immunoprecipitation with GFP-BCL9.
source: coIP assays revealed robust binding between HA-tagged TLE3 (HA-TLE) and wt GFP-BCL9 but not with two different C-terminal truncations (Figure 5B). Indeed, the C-terminal WD40 domain of TLE3 is both necessary and sufficient for this coIP (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an observation from co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: The WD40 domain of TLE3 binds to short motifs within a range of DNA-binding repressors.
source: This domain binds to short motifs within a range of DNA-binding repressors (Jennings et al., 2006), but is not involved in binding to TCF (Chodaparambil et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a fact from previous literature supported by citations.

claim: The WD40 domain of TLE3 is not involved in binding to TCF.
source: This domain binds to short motifs within a range of DNA-binding repressors (Jennings et al., 2006), but is not involved in binding to TCF (Chodaparambil et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a fact from previous literature supported by citation.

claim: BCL9/B9L could bind directly to TCF-associated TLE/Groucho.
source: Therefore, BCL9/B9L could bind directly to TCF-associated TLE/Groucho (as indicated by RIME, see above).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the coIP and RIME data.

claim: LDB1 association with B9L-BirA* is reduced by half compared to wild-type control when HD3 is deleted.
source: Likewise, a small number of proteins show reduced association with BCL9 or B9L baits lacking HD3, with the top hit being LDB1 whose association with B9L-BirA* is reduced by half compared to the wt control (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Binding between LDB1-FLAG and GFP-B9L is significantly reduced if HD3 is deleted.
source: Indeed, binding between LDB1-FLAG and GFP-B9L, GFP-BCL9 or GFP-Lgs is readily detectable in coIP assays, but is significantly reduced if HD3 is deleted (Figure 5E; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Binding between LDB1-FLAG and GFP-BCL9/B9L is similarly reduced by an alanine substitution of W472 in BCL9 or W520 in B9L.
source: Binding is similarly reduced by an alanine substitution of the most conserved residue in HD3 (W472 in BCL9, W520 in B9L; see also below), and eliminated if △HD1 is tested (Figure 5E; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: HD3 and HD1 are important for the interaction between ChiLS and BCL9/B9L.
source: This indicates the importance of HD3 and HD1 for the interaction between ChiLS and BCL9/B9L, whereby HD1 likely contributes indirectly to this interaction via its binding to PYGO2 (Figure 5A) (Fiedler et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the coIP experiments with HD3 and HD1 deletions.

claim: HD1 likely contributes indirectly to the interaction between ChiLS and BCL9/B9L via its binding to PYGO2.
source: This indicates the importance of HD3 and HD1 for the interaction between ChiLS and BCL9/B9L, whereby HD1 likely contributes indirectly to this interaction via its binding to PYGO2 (Figure 5A) (Fiedler et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known binding of HD1 to PYGO2 and the BioID data.

claim: ChiLS co-immunoprecipitates less efficiently with BCL9 in the absence of Pygo.
source: We generated PYGO2 KO cells by CRISPR/Cas9 (noting that HEK293T cells do not express PYGO1), to confirm that ChiLS coIPs less efficiently with BCL9 in the absence of Pygo (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from co-immunoprecipitation experiments in PYGO2 KO cells shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pygo promotes the association between BCL9/B9L and ChiLS.
source: This supports the notion that Pygo promotes the association between BCL9/B9L and ChiLS.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the coIP experiments in PYGO2 KO cells.

claim: HD3 is predicted to form a single α-helix.
source: Next, we asked whether HD3 is a direct binding site for ChiLS. This short conserved element is predicted to form a single α-helix (Peng and Xu, 2011), with an invariant tryptophan and a phenylalanine/tyrosine (F/Y) doublet further downstream whose hydrophobic side chains extend in the same direction (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is a structural prediction from the literature supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 6A,B.

claim: HD3 has an invariant tryptophan and a phenylalanine/tyrosine doublet whose hydrophobic side chains extend in the same direction.
source: Next, we asked whether HD3 is a direct binding site for ChiLS. This short conserved element is predicted to form a single α-helix (Peng and Xu, 2011), with an invariant tryptophan and a phenylalanine/tyrosine (F/Y) doublet further downstream whose hydrophobic side chains extend in the same direction (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is a structural observation illustrated in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The invariant tryptophan and phenylalanine/tyrosine doublet in HD3 form a hydrophobic surface to which ChiLS may bind.
source: Together, they form a hydrophobic surface to which ChiLS may bind.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the structural features of HD3.

claim: Incubation of 15N-Lip-HD3 with purified ChiLS complex produces clear line broadening of selective peaks.
source: 15N-Lip-HD3 proved soluble and monomeric (as judged by size exclusion chromatography), and produces well-dispersed heteronuclear single-quantum correlation (HSQC) spectra. Incubation of 15N-Lip-HD3 with purified ChiLS complex, but not with purified SSDP alone, produces clear line broadening ('bleaching') of selective peaks (Figure 6D,E) – strong evidence for a direct interaction.
evidence: This is an observation from NMR binding assays shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Incubation of 15N-Lip-HD3 with purified SSDP alone does not produce line broadening.
source: 15N-Lip-HD3 proved soluble and monomeric (as judged by size exclusion chromatography), and produces well-dispersed heteronuclear single-quantum correlation (HSQC) spectra. Incubation of 15N-Lip-HD3 with purified ChiLS complex, but not with purified SSDP alone, produces clear line broadening ('bleaching') of selective peaks (Figure 6D,E) – strong evidence for a direct interaction.
evidence: This is an observation from NMR binding assays shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The line broadening of 15N-Lip-HD3 upon incubation with ChiLS is strong evidence for a direct interaction.
source: Incubation of 15N-Lip-HD3 with purified ChiLS complex, but not with purified SSDP alone, produces clear line broadening ('bleaching') of selective peaks (Figure 6D,E) – strong evidence for a direct interaction.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the NMR data.

claim: HD3 is helical in nature.
source: Assignments of these peaks (obtained with a double-labeled 13C15N-Lip-HD3 sample; Figure 6—figure supplement 1) provided experimental evidence for the helical nature of HD3 (as ascertained by TALOS+; Shen et al., 2009) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is an observation from NMR experiments shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most residues of HD3 are implicated in the interaction with ChiLS.
source: It allowed us to generate a heat-map that implicates most residues of HD3 in the interaction with ChiLS (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is an observation from NMR experiments illustrated in Figure 6B.

claim: No spectral changes are observed if a W520R-mutant version of 15N-Lip-HD3 is incubated with ChiLS.
source: Importantly, no spectral changes are observed if a W520R-mutant version of 15N-Lip-HD3 is incubated with ChiLS (Figure 6F), showing that this point mutation abrogates the binding of HD3 to ChiLS.
evidence: This is an observation from NMR experiments shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The W520R point mutation abrogates the binding of HD3 to ChiLS.
source: Importantly, no spectral changes are observed if a W520R-mutant version of 15N-Lip-HD3 is incubated with ChiLS (Figure 6F), showing that this point mutation abrogates the binding of HD3 to ChiLS.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the NMR data with the W520R mutant.

claim: ChiLS binds directly and specifically to HD3.
source: Thus, ChiLS binds directly and specifically to HD3.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the NMR binding assays.

claim: Flies heterozygous for chip exhibit multiple wing notches.
source: Given this physical interaction between HD3 and ChiLS, we asked whether we could also detect genetic interactions between lgs and chip in Drosophila. Flies heterozygous for chip exhibit multiple wing notches (Shoresh et al., 1998) that are strongly exacerbated by heterozygosity of ssdp; however, this phenotype is ameliorated by heterozygosity of several Wnt signaling components including pygo, groucho and lgs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a genetic observation from Drosophila experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2, supported by citation.

claim: The wing notch phenotype of chip heterozygotes is strongly exacerbated by heterozygosity of ssdp.
source: Given this physical interaction between HD3 and ChiLS, we asked whether we could also detect genetic interactions between lgs and chip in Drosophila. Flies heterozygous for chip exhibit multiple wing notches (Shoresh et al., 1998) that are strongly exacerbated by heterozygosity of ssdp; however, this phenotype is ameliorated by heterozygosity of several Wnt signaling components including pygo, groucho and lgs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a genetic observation from Drosophila experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The wing notch phenotype of chip heterozygotes is ameliorated by heterozygosity of several Wnt signaling components including pygo, groucho and lgs.
source: Given this physical interaction between HD3 and ChiLS, we asked whether we could also detect genetic interactions between lgs and chip in Drosophila. Flies heterozygous for chip exhibit multiple wing notches (Shoresh et al., 1998) that are strongly exacerbated by heterozygosity of ssdp; however, this phenotype is ameliorated by heterozygosity of several Wnt signaling components including pygo, groucho and lgs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a genetic observation from Drosophila experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Heterozygosity of lgsΔHD3 restores normal wing margins in more than 25% of chip heterozygous flies.
source: Interestingly, the strongest interaction is seen with lgsΔHD3 whose heterozygosity restores normal margins in >25% of the flies.
evidence: This is a quantitative genetic observation from Drosophila experiments.

claim: Strong genetic interactions between chip and HD3-defective lgs alleles underscore the close functional link between these two proteins.
source: These strong genetic interactions between chip and HD3-defective lgs alleles further underscore the close functional link between these two proteins.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic interaction data.

claim: BioID experiments consistently found multiple components of nuclear co-receptor complexes amongst the top hits for all three BirA* baits.
source: Unexpectedly, we consistently found multiple components of nuclear co-receptors complexes amongst the top hits for all three BirA* baits, including several NCOA co-activators and NCOR co-repressors (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: BioID experiments with B9L-BirA* found the arylhydrocarbon receptor (AHR) and its partner ARNT.
source: In the case of B9L-BirA*, we also found the DNA-binding components of the resident complex, namely the arylhydrocarbon receptor (AHR) and its partner ARNT (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from BioID mass spectrometry experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There is close proximity between BCL9/B9L-PYGO2 and nuclear co-receptor complexes.
source: Clearly, there is close proximity between BCL9/B9L-PYGO2 and nuclear co-receptor complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the BioID data.

claim: A substantial fraction of Wnt-responsive enhancers also contain binding sites for nuclear receptors near TCF-binding sites.
source: This suggests that a substantial fraction of Wnt-responsive enhancers also contain binding sites for nuclear receptors (for example, AHR in HEK293T cells), and that these sites are near TCF-binding sites.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the BioID data showing proximity between BCL9/B9L-PYGO2 and nuclear co-receptor complexes.

claim: ChiLS is a direct and specific ligand of the α-helical HD3 element of B9L and likely of other Legless/BCL9 orthologs.
source: The first of these is ChiLS, the core module of the Wnt enhanceosome (Fiedler et al., 2015) (Figure 7): we have shown that ChiLS is a direct and specific ligand of the α-helical HD3 element of B9L and, likely, of other Legless/BCL9 orthologs, given the strong sequence conservation of this α-helix (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the NMR binding assays and sequence conservation analysis.

claim: The physiological relevance of the interaction between HD3 and ChiLS is underscored by genetic analysis in flies.
source: The physiological relevance of this interaction with ChiLS is underscored by genetic analysis in flies.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic interaction data from Drosophila.

claim: HD3 is an evolutionary conserved contact point between Legless/BCL9 and ChiLS.
source: Our evidence thus implicates HD3 as an evolutionary conserved contact point between Legless/BCL9 and ChiLS, although the primary link between these two proteins appears to be provided by Pygo.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the NMR, coIP, and genetic data.

claim: The primary link between Legless/BCL9 and ChiLS appears to be provided by Pygo.
source: Our evidence thus implicates HD3 as an evolutionary conserved contact point between Legless/BCL9 and ChiLS, although the primary link between these two proteins appears to be provided by Pygo.
evidence: This is an inference based on the coIP data showing reduced binding in the absence of Pygo.

claim: Legless/BCL9 undergoes three separate functionally relevant interactions with distinct components of the Wnt enhanceosome—with Pygo, ChiLS and Groucho/TLE.
source: Our evidence indicates that Legless/BCL9 undergoes three separate functionally relevant interactions with distinct components of the Wnt enhanceosome—with Pygo, ChiLS and Groucho/TLE (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary of the findings illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The interactions between Legless/BCL9 and Pygo, ChiLS, and Groucho/TLE are constitutive, preceding Wnt signaling.
source: Importantly, BioID revealed that these interactions are constitutive, preceding Wnt signaling, and that they hardly change upon Wnt stimulation (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the BioID data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Legless/BCL9 is a core component of the Wnt enhanceosome, providing a scaffolding function that facilitates its assembly and/or maintains its cohesion.
source: Taken together with its multivalent interactions with the Wnt enhanceosome, this is consistent with Legless/BCL9 being a core component of this complex, providing a scaffolding function that facilitates its assembly and/or maintains its cohesion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the multivalent interactions and constitutive association of Legless/BCL9 with the enhanceosome.

claim: Legless/BCL9 confers Wnt-responsiveness on the Wnt enhanceosome through its ability to capture Armadillo/β-catenin.
source: Following Wnt stimulation, Legless/BCL9 undergoes an additional physiologically relevant interaction, by binding to (stabilized) Armadillo/β-catenin via HD2 (Kramps et al., 2002). Legless/BCL9 thus confers Wnt-responsiveness on the Wnt enhanceosome through its ability to capture Armadillo/β-catenin.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the known binding of Legless/BCL9 to β-catenin and the functional data.

claim: Legless/BCL9 earmarks the Wnt enhanceosome for Wnt responses.
source: In other words, in addition to scaffolding the enhanceosome, Legless/BCL9 also earmarks this complex for Wnt responses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the dual role of Legless/BCL9 in scaffolding and capturing β-catenin.

claim: The capture of β-catenin by Legless/BCL9 triggers its rearrangement within the complex, apposing its C-terminus to TCF.
source: Intriguingly, our BioID data indicated that the capture of β-catenin by Legless/BCL9 triggers its rearrangement within the complex, apposing its C-terminus to TCF (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the BioID data showing β-catenin-dependent proximity changes, illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The β-catenin-dependent apposition of the Legless/BCL9 C-terminus to TCF is consistent with structural data showing that BCL9/B9L HD2 is closely apposed to TCF when in a ternary complex with β-catenin.
source: This apparent β-catenin-dependent apposition is consistent with structural data showing that BCL9/B9L HD2 is closely apposed to TCF when in a ternary complex with β-catenin (Sampietro et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a comparison of the BioID findings with previous structural data supported by citation.

claim: The β-catenin-dependent apposition of the Legless/BCL9 C-terminus to TCF is likely to trigger Wnt enhanceosome switching from OFF to ON.
source: Whatever the case, the β-catenin-dependent apposition of the Legless/BCL9 C-terminus to TCF is likely to trigger Wnt enhanceosome switching from OFF to ON, resulting in the relief of Groucho/TLE-dependent repression and culminating in the Wnt-dependent transcriptional activation of linked target genes (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of enhanceosome switching based on the BioID data, illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The transition of the Wnt enhanceosome from OFF to ON is accompanied by a proximity gain between Legless/BCL9 and CBP/p300.
source: This transition of the Wnt enhanceosome from OFF to ON is accompanied by a proximity gain between Legless/BCL9 and CBP/p300 (Figure 4), likely to reflect at least in part its de novo binding to Armadillo/β-catenin.
evidence: This is an observation from BioID experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: CBP/p300 is associated with the Wnt enhanceosome prior to Wnt signaling.
source: However, our evidence indicates that CBP/p300 is associated with the Wnt enhanceosome prior to Wnt signaling, possibly via direct binding to B9L as suggested by RIME (Figure 4C), and that the docking of Armadillo/β-catenin to the Wnt enhanceosome strengthens its association with CBP/p300, and/or directs the histone acetyltransferase activity of CBP/p300 towards its substrates, primarily the histone tails.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the BioID and RIME data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CBP/p300 appears to promote Wnt-dependent transcription in flies and human cells by acetylating histone tails.
source: By acetylating these tails, CBP/p300 appears to promote Wnt-dependent transcription in flies and human cells (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a conclusion from previous literature supported by citation.

claim: CBP-dependent histone acetylation has been observed at Wg target enhancers in Drosophila, preceding transcriptional activation.
source: Indeed, CBP-dependent histone acetylation has been observed at Wg target enhancers in Drosophila although, interestingly, this preceded transcriptional activation (Parker et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a fact from previous literature supported by citation.

claim: Histone acetylation at Wnt target enhancers is instrumental in antagonizing the compaction of their chromatin imposed by Groucho/TLE.
source: It seems plausible that histone acetylation at Wnt target enhancers is instrumental in antagonizing the compaction of their chromatin imposed by Groucho/TLE, which depends on its tetramerization via its Q domain (Chodaparambil et al., 2014) as well as its binding to HDACs (Jennings et al., 2008; Turki-Judeh and Courey, 2012).
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of chromatin decompaction supported by citations.

claim: CBP/p300 has non-histone substrates within the Wnt enhanceosome, including dTCF in Drosophila.
source: However, CBP/p300 also has non-histone substrates within the Wnt enhanceosome, including dTCF in Drosophila whose Armadillo-binding site can be acetylated by dCBP, which thus blocks the binding between the two proteins (Waltzer and Bienz, 1998) and antagonizes Wg responses (Li et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a fact from previous literature supported by citations.

claim: CBP/p300 regulates Wnt-dependent transcription positively as well as negatively.
source: It thus regulates Wnt-dependent transcription positively as well as negatively, similarly to Groucho/TLE which not only silences Wnt target genes but also earmarks them for Wnt inducibility, as a core component of the Wnt enhanceosome.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the dual roles of CBP/p300 in Wnt signaling.

claim: Groucho/TLE not only silences Wnt target genes but also earmarks them for Wnt inducibility, as a core component of the Wnt enhanceosome.
source: It thus regulates Wnt-dependent transcription positively as well as negatively, similarly to Groucho/TLE which not only silences Wnt target genes but also earmarks them for Wnt inducibility, as a core component of the Wnt enhanceosome.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the dual roles of Groucho/TLE in the Wnt enhanceosome model.

claim: Both CBP/p300 and Groucho/TLE are associated constitutively with the Wnt enhanceosome.
source: It is intriguing that both bimodal regulators are associated constitutively with this complex.
evidence: This is an observation from the BioID data.

claim: The docking of Armadillo/β-catenin to the Wnt enhanceosome changes the substrate specificities and/or activities of CBP/p300 and Groucho/TLE.
source: A corollary is that the docking of Armadillo/β-catenin to the Wnt enhanceosome changes their substrate specificities and/or activities.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the bimodal regulatory roles of CBP/p300 and Groucho/TLE.

claim: The BAF complex appears to be a constitutive component of the Wnt enhanceosome.
source: An important refinement of our initial enhanceosome model is with regard to the BAF complex, which appears to be a constitutive component of the Wnt enhanceosome (Figure 7), as indicated by our BioID data.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the BioID data illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The BAF complex primarily antagonizes Polycomb-mediated silencing of genes.
source: A wealth of evidence from studies in flies and mammals indicates that this complex primarily antagonizes Polycomb-mediated silencing of genes, most notably of the INK4A locus which encodes an anti-proliferative factor, which could explain why the BAF complex functions as a tumor suppressor in many tissues.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the BAF complex function.

claim: The BAF complex specifically antagonizes Armadillo/β-catenin-mediated transcription.
source: However, recall that this complex also specifically antagonizes Armadillo/β-catenin-mediated transcription (Collins and Treisman, 2000), likely via its BRG/BRM subunit which directly binds to β-catenin (Barker et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a fact from previous literature supported by citations.

claim: The BAF complex mediates a negative feedback from high Wg signaling levels near Wg-producing cells which results in re-repression.
source: Evidence from studies in Drosophila of Wg-responsive enhancers suggests that this complex mediates a negative feedback from high Wg signaling levels near Wg-producing cells which results in re-repression (Collins and Treisman, 2000), imposed by the Brinker homeodomain repressor (Saller et al., 2002; Waltzer et al., 2001; Theisen et al., 2007) and its Armadillo-binding Teashirt co-repressor (Gallet et al., 1999) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion from previous literature supported by citations, illustrated in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The BAF complex may also instal silencing on Wnt-responsive enhancers upon cessation of Wnt signaling.
source: The same factors may also instal silencing on Wnt-responsive enhancers upon cessation of Wnt signaling.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the role of the BAF complex in feedback inhibition.

claim: Mammals do not have a Brinker ortholog.
source: Notably, mammals do not have a Brinker ortholog, which could explain some of the apparent functional differences between flies and mammals with regard to the BAF complex (Kadoch and Crabtree, 2015).
evidence: This is a fact about evolutionary conservation.

claim: The closest mammalian relatives of Teashirt are the Homothorax/MEIS proteins.
source: However, the closest mammalian relatives of Teashirt are the Homothorax/MEIS proteins, a family of homeodomain proteins whose expression can be Wnt-inducible (for example, Wernet et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a fact about evolutionary relationships supported by citation.

claim: Homothorax/MEIS proteins are candidates for Wnt-induced repressors that confer BAF-dependent feedback inhibition.
source: They are thus candidates for Wnt-induced repressors that confer BAF-dependent feedback inhibition.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the evolutionary relationship and Wnt-inducible expression of MEIS proteins.

claim: None of the BioID lists contained RUNX proteins.
source: Notably, none of our BioID lists contained RUNX proteins.
evidence: This is an observation from the BioID mass spectrometry data.

claim: RUNX proteins are pivotal for initial assembly of the Wnt enhanceosome at Wnt-responsive enhancers during early embryonic development, or in uncommitted progenitor cells of specific cell lineages.
source: Based on our functional evidence from Drosophila midgut enhancers, we proposed that these proteins (which bind to both enhancers and Groucho/TLE) are pivotal for initial assembly of the Wnt enhanceosome at Wnt-responsive enhancers during early embryonic development, or in uncommitted progenitor cells of specific cell lineages (Fiedler et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a model proposed by the authors based on previous work supported by citation.

claim: HEK293 cells may not express any RUNX factors.
source: However, HEK293 cells are epithelial cells and may thus not express any RUNX factors.
evidence: This is a speculation about gene expression in HEK293 cells.

claim: RUNX factors function in a hit-and-run fashion.
source: In any case, our negative BioID results suggest that RUNX factors function in a hit-and-run fashion.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the absence of RUNX proteins in the BioID data.

claim: The Wnt enhanceosome complex, once assembled at Wnt-responsive enhancers, can switch between ON and OFF states without RUNX.
source: Evidently, the Wnt enhanceosome complex, once assembled at Wnt-responsive enhancers, can switch between ON and OFF states without RUNX.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the absence of RUNX proteins in the BioID data from HEK293 cells.

claim: Legless/BCL9 has a fundamental role as a scaffold of the Wnt enhanceosome, far beyond its role in linking Armadillo/β-catenin to Pygo.
source: In summary, we have uncovered a fundamental role to Legless/BCL9 as a scaffold of the Wnt enhanceosome, far beyond its role in linking Armadillo/β-catenin to Pygo.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: The function of Legless/BCL9 may extend beyond transcriptional Wnt responses.
source: Indeed, the function of Legless/BCL9 may extend beyond transcriptional Wnt responses, as indicated by the unexpected discovery of its strong association with nuclear co-receptor complexes.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the BioID data showing association with nuclear co-receptor complexes.

claim: There is documented cross-talk between Wnt/β-catenin and nuclear hormone receptor signaling.
source: Potentially, these associations underlie the observed cross-talk between Wnt/β-catenin and nuclear hormone receptor signaling, documented extensively in the literature (for example, Beildeck et al., 2010; Mulholland et al., 2005; Schneider et al., 2014), including evidence for direct activation of the androgen receptor by β-catenin (Kypta and Waxman, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: There is evidence for direct activation of the androgen receptor by β-catenin.
source: Potentially, these associations underlie the observed cross-talk between Wnt/β-catenin and nuclear hormone receptor signaling, documented extensively in the literature (for example, Beildeck et al., 2010; Mulholland et al., 2005; Schneider et al., 2014), including evidence for direct activation of the androgen receptor by β-catenin (Kypta and Waxman, 2012).
evidence: This is a fact from previous literature supported by citation.

claim: A strong association between TLE1 and the estrogen receptor has been discovered in breast cancer cells.
source: Furthermore, a strong association between TLE1 and the estrogen receptor has been discovered in breast cancer cells, where TLE1 assists the estrogen receptor in its interaction with chromatin and its proliferation-promoting function (Holmes et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a fact from previous literature supported by citation.

claim: TLE1 assists the estrogen receptor in its interaction with chromatin and its proliferation-promoting function in breast cancer cells.
source: Furthermore, a strong association between TLE1 and the estrogen receptor has been discovered in breast cancer cells, where TLE1 assists the estrogen receptor in its interaction with chromatin and its proliferation-promoting function (Holmes et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a fact from previous literature supported by citation.
